claim: Peptidoglycans (PGNs) are immunogenic bacterial surface patterns that trigger immune activation in metazoans and plants.
source: Peptidoglycans (PGNs) are immunogenic bacterial surface patterns that trigger immune activation in metazoans and plants.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana produces a metazoan lysozyme-like hydrolase (lysozyme 1, LYS1) upon bacterial infection or exposure to microbial patterns.
source: Here we show that Arabidopsis thaliana, upon bacterial infection or exposure to microbial patterns, produces a metazoan lysozyme-like hydrolase (lysozyme 1, LYS1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including expression analysis and enzymatic assays.

claim: LYS1 activity releases soluble PGN fragments from insoluble bacterial cell walls.
source: LYS1 activity releases soluble PGN fragments from insoluble bacterial cell walls and cleavage products are able to trigger responses typically associated with plant immunity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PGN degradation assays and HPLC analysis of cleavage products.

claim: LYS1 cleavage products are able to trigger responses typically associated with plant immunity.
source: LYS1 activity releases soluble PGN fragments from insoluble bacterial cell walls and cleavage products are able to trigger responses typically associated with plant immunity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immune response assays showing FRK1 gene expression and medium alkalinization.

claim: LYS1 mutant genotypes exhibit super-susceptibility to bacterial infections similar to that observed on PGN receptor mutants.
source: Importantly, LYS1 mutant genotypes exhibit super-susceptibility to bacterial infections similar to that observed on PGN receptor mutants.
evidence: This is supported by bacterial infection assays comparing LYS1 knock-down lines with wild-type and PGN receptor mutants.

claim: Bacteria-derived PAMPs such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) or flagellins possess immunity-stimulating activities in metazoans and plants.
source: Bacteria-derived PAMPs such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) or flagellins possess immunity-stimulating activities in metazoans and plants, suggesting that the ability to sense bacterial surface structures and mount immunity is conserved across lineage borders (Nürnberger et al., 2004; Boller and Felix, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ability to sense bacterial surface structures and mount immunity is conserved across lineage borders.
source: Bacteria-derived PAMPs such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS) or flagellins possess immunity-stimulating activities in metazoans and plants, suggesting that the ability to sense bacterial surface structures and mount immunity is conserved across lineage borders (Nürnberger et al., 2004; Boller and Felix, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that similar PAMPs trigger immunity in different organisms.

claim: PGNs are major building blocks of the cell walls of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Likewise, peptidoglycans (PGNs) are major building blocks of the cell walls of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria that have been shown to trigger host immune responses in mammalians, insects, and plants (Dziarski and Gupta, 2005; Gust et al., 2007; Erbs et al., 2008; Kurata, 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial cell wall structure.

claim: PGNs have been shown to trigger host immune responses in mammalians, insects, and plants.
source: Likewise, peptidoglycans (PGNs) are major building blocks of the cell walls of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria that have been shown to trigger host immune responses in mammalians, insects, and plants (Dziarski and Gupta, 2005; Gust et al., 2007; Erbs et al., 2008; Kurata, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: PGNs are heteroglycan chains that are composed of polymeric alternating β(1,4)-linked N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) residues.
source: Structurally, PGNs are heteroglycan chains that are composed of polymeric alternating β(1,4)-linked N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) residues (Schleifer and Kandler, 1972; Glauner et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about PGN supported by citations.

claim: PGN chains are interconnected by oligopeptide bridges which form a coordinate meshwork, thereby providing structural integrity to the bacterial envelope.
source: Such chains are interconnected by oligopeptide bridges which form a coordinate meshwork, thereby providing structural integrity to the bacterial envelope.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PGN structure and function.

claim: Recognition of different PGN substructures in animal hosts is brought about by structurally diverse PRRs such as nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing proteins (NODs), peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs/PGLYRPs), scavenger receptors, or Toll-like receptor TLR2.
source: Recognition of different PGN substructures in animal hosts is brought about by structurally diverse PRRs such as nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing proteins (NODs), peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs/PGLYRPs), scavenger receptors, or Toll-like receptor TLR2 (Strober et al., 2006; Royet and Dziarski, 2007; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Müller-Anstett et al., 2010; Magalhaes et al., 2011; Kurata, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research on animal PGN recognition systems.

claim: A tripartite PGN recognition system at the plasma membrane of Arabidopsis thaliana with shared functions in PGN sensing and transmembrane signaling was recently described.
source: In plants, a tripartite PGN recognition system at the plasma membrane of Arabidopsis thaliana with shared functions in PGN sensing and transmembrane signaling was recently described (Willmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The Arabidopsis PGN recognition system comprises Lysin motif (LysM) domain proteins LYM1 and LYM3 for PGN ligand binding and the transmembrane LysM receptor kinase CERK1 that is likely required for conveying the extracellular signal across the plasma membrane and for initiating intracellular signal transduction.
source: This system comprises Lysin motif (LysM) domain proteins LYM1 and LYM3 for PGN ligand binding and the transmembrane LysM receptor kinase CERK1 that is likely required for conveying the extracellular signal across the plasma membrane and for initiating intracellular signal transduction.
evidence: This is based on previous research cited in the manuscript.

claim: All three proteins (LYM1, LYM3, CERK1) were shown to be indispensable for PGN sensitivity and to contribute to immunity to bacterial infection.
source: All three proteins were shown to be indispensable for PGN sensitivity and to contribute to immunity to bacterial infection (Willmann et al., 2011), which is in agreement with their proposed role as a PGN sensor system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A similar PGN perception system made of LysM domain proteins LYP4 and LYP6 has been reported from rice.
source: More recently, a similar PGN perception system made of LysM domain proteins LYP4 and LYP6 has been reported from rice (Liu et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Recognition by host PRRs most likely requires the presence of soluble, randomly structured ligands derived from a complex matrix.
source: It is therefore assumed that recognition by host PRRs most likely requires the presence of soluble, randomly structured ligands derived from a complex matrix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural nature of microbial patterns and PRR binding requirements.

claim: X-ray structure-based insight into the binding of bacterial flagellin to the Arabidopsis receptor complex FLS2/BAK1 or of fungal chitin to the Arabidopsis receptor CERK1 supports the view that recognition requires soluble ligands.
source: X-ray structure-based insight into the binding of bacterial flagellin to the Arabidopsis receptor complex FLS2/BAK1 or of fungal chitin to the Arabidopsis receptor CERK1 supports this view (Willmann and Nürnberger, 2012; Liu et al., 2012b; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The existence of fungal LysM effector proteins that scavenge soluble chitin fragments, thus preventing recognition by plant PRRs, suggests that mechanisms releasing these soluble fragments from fungal cell walls must exist.
source: Moreover, the existence of fungal LysM effector proteins that scavenge soluble chitin fragments, thus preventing recognition by plant PRRs, suggests that mechanisms releasing these soluble fragments from fungal cell walls must exist (de Jonge et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of effector proteins that sequester chitin fragments, supported by a citation.

claim: Only monomers of bacterial flagellin induce immune responses through human TLR5 whereas filamentous flagella do not.
source: For example, only monomers of bacterial flagellin induce immune responses through human TLR5 whereas filamentous flagella, in which the immunogenic flagellin structure is buried and thus is not accessible to TLR5, do not (Smith et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Caulobacter crescentus deliberately ejects its flagellum once it is no longer required for the bacterial life cycle.
source: For instance, Caulobacter crescentus deliberately ejects its flagellum once it is no longer required for the bacterial life cycle (Jenal and Stephens, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During infection, Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces rhamnolipids which act as surfactants and cause flagellin shedding from intact flagella, resulting in a more pronounced immune response.
source: Moreover, during infection, Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces rhamnolipids which act as surfactants and cause flagellin shedding from intact flagella, resulting in a more pronounced immune response (Gerstel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Host factors such as proteases or environmental conditions such as pH, temperature, or bile salts have been proposed to mediate shearing of flagella from bacterial surfaces.
source: Alternatively, host factors such as proteases or environmental conditions such as pH, temperature, or bile salts have been proposed to mediate shearing of flagella from bacterial surfaces (Ramos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Animal lysozymes have been implicated in PGN hydrolysis, bacterial lysis, and host immunity.
source: Animal lysozymes have been implicated in PGN hydrolysis, bacterial lysis, and host immunity (Callewaert and Michiels, 2010), probably through partial PGN degradation and generation of soluble ligands for PGN sensors (Cho et al., 2005; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Animal lysozymes probably contribute to immunity through partial PGN degradation and generation of soluble ligands for PGN sensors.
source: Animal lysozymes have been implicated in PGN hydrolysis, bacterial lysis, and host immunity (Callewaert and Michiels, 2010), probably through partial PGN degradation and generation of soluble ligands for PGN sensors (Cho et al., 2005; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recombinant Arabidopsis PGN binding proteins LYM1 and LYM3 do not catalyze PGN degradation.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, lysozyme, but not recombinant LYM1 or LYM3, displayed cell wall-degrading lytic activity, suggesting that the latter are unable to release PGN fragments from bacterial cell walls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LYM1 and LYM3 lack sequence similarities with known metazoan PGN hydrolytic activities.
source: This is in agreement with a lack of sequence similarities between LYM1 or LYM3 and known metazoan PGN hydrolytic activities.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: LYM1 and LYM3 constitute plant PGN sensors that appear to be functionally related to non-enzymatic mammalian or Drosophila PGRPs.
source: We therefore conclude that LYM1 and LYM3 constitute plant PGN sensors that appear to be functionally related to non-enzymatic mammalian or Drosophila PGRPs (Cho et al., 2005; Bischoff et al., 2006; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Kurata, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of enzymatic activity and comparison with animal PGRPs, supported by citations.

claim: Lysozymes hydrolyze β(1,4) linkages between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine residues in PGNs and between N-acetylglucosamine residues in chitodextrins.
source: Lysozymes (EC 3.2.1.17) hydrolyze β(1,4) linkages between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine residues in PGNs and between N-acetylglucosamine residues in chitodextrins (http://enzyme.expasy.org/EC/3.2.1.17).
evidence: This is established knowledge about lysozyme enzymatic activity.

claim: Plant genomes do not encode lysozyme-like proteins, but many plant species produce lysozyme-like enzyme activities such as chitinases.
source: Plant genomes do not encode lysozyme-like proteins, but many plant species produce lysozyme-like enzyme activities such as chitinases (EC 3.2.1.14) (Audy et al., 1988; Sakthivel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plant chitinases fall into five classes (I–V).
source: Plant chitinases fall into five classes (I–V, Figure 1B) (Passarinho and de Vries, 2002) and are grouped into structurally unrelated families 18 and 19 of glycosyl hydrolases, respectively (Henrissat, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Chitinases belonging to family 18 of glycosyl hydrolases are ubiquitously found in all organisms.
source: Chitinases belonging to family 18 of glycosyl hydrolases are ubiquitously found in all organisms whereas chitinases of glycosyl hydrolase family 19 are found almost exclusively in plants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chitinase distribution.

claim: Chitinases of glycosyl hydrolase family 19 are found almost exclusively in plants.
source: Chitinases belonging to family 18 of glycosyl hydrolases are ubiquitously found in all organisms whereas chitinases of glycosyl hydrolase family 19 are found almost exclusively in plants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chitinase distribution.

claim: Class III chitinases represent bifunctional plant enzymes with lysozyme-like activities.
source: Class III chitinases (glycosyl hydrolase family 18) represent bifunctional plant enzymes with lysozyme-like activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about class III chitinases.

claim: Hevamine from the rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis has been shown to hydrolyze PGN and the structurally closely related β(1,4)-linked GlcNAc homopolymer chitin in vitro.
source: One such enzyme, hevamine from the rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis (Beintema et al., 1991), has been shown to hydrolyze PGN and the structurally closely related β(1,4)-linked GlcNAc homopolymer chitin in vitro (Bokma et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LYS1 (At5g24090) represents the only class III chitinase encoded by the Arabidopsis genome.
source: To explore host-mediated PGN degradation and its possible implication in plant immune activation, we have addressed the only class III chitinase (which we named LYS1, At5g24090) encoded by the Arabidopsis genome (Passarinho and de Vries, 2002; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on genome analysis and supported by a citation, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: LYS1 gene expression is enhanced upon infection with host non-adapted Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (Pph) or disarmed host adapted P. syringae pv. tomato (Pto) DC3000 hrcC−.
source: Bacterial infection of Arabidopsis plants stably expressing a pLYS1::GUS construct revealed that LYS1 gene expression is enhanced upon infection with host non-adapted Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (Pph) or disarmed host adapted P. syringae pv. tomato (Pto) DC3000 hrcC−.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GUS reporter assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of the immune response marker pathogenesis-related protein 1 (PR1) was enhanced by infection with Pph or Pto DC3000 hrcC−.
source: Likewise, expression of the immune response marker pathogenesis-related protein 1 (PR1) was enhanced by the same treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GUS reporter assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Failure to detect LYS1 expression in plants infected with virulent host adapted Pto DC3000 suggests bacterial effector-mediated suppression.
source: Failure to detect LYS1 expression in plants infected with virulent host adapted Pto DC3000 suggests bacterial effector-mediated suppression that is reminiscent of that observed for PGN receptor proteins LYM1 and LYM3 (Willmann et al., 2011) as well as numerous other immunity-associated genes (Kemmerling et al., 2007; Postel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of expression during virulent infection, supported by citations to similar observations.

claim: LYS1 gene expression is triggered upon treatment with different MAMPs including bacterial flagellin, LPS, or PGN preparations.
source: LYS1 gene expression is not only triggered upon bacterial infection, but was also observed upon treatment with different MAMPs including bacterial flagellin, LPS, or PGN preparations (Figure 1D), similar to the immune marker gene Flagellin-responsive kinase 1 (FRK1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Infection-induced LYS1 transcriptional activation suggests that the LYS1 protein is implicated in immunity to bacterial infection.
source: Altogether, infection-induced LYS1 transcriptional activation suggests that the LYS1 protein is implicated in immunity to bacterial infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of LYS1 expression during infection.

claim: Overexpression of LYS1 in E. coli failed to produce active enzyme.
source: Overexpression in Escherichia coli failed to produce active enzyme and LYS1 production in eukaryotic Pichia pastoris entirely failed to produce recombinant protein (not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental attempts to produce recombinant protein.

claim: LYS1 production in eukaryotic Pichia pastoris entirely failed to produce recombinant protein.
source: Overexpression in Escherichia coli failed to produce active enzyme and LYS1 production in eukaryotic Pichia pastoris entirely failed to produce recombinant protein (not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental attempts to produce recombinant protein.

claim: LYS1-GFP is glycosylated.
source: Notably, LYS1-GFP was glycosylated (Figure 2C), possibly explaining the failure to produce enzymatically active LYS1 protein in E. coli.
evidence: This is demonstrated by deglycosylation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of the LYS1-GFP fusion protein in Arabidopsis plants was accompanied by substantial proteolytic cleavage resulting in the predominant release of a protein with an approximate molecular mass of 35 kDa, most likely representing untagged LYS1.
source: Expression of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion protein in Arabidopsis plants was accompanied by substantial proteolytic cleavage resulting in the predominant release of a protein with an approximate molecular mass of 35 kDa, most likely representing untagged LYS1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LC-MS/MS analysis confirmed the identity of LYS1 in the 35 kDa band and yielded peptides spanning the whole protein sequence, except for the first 53 amino acids.
source: Analysis of this major cleavage product by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) after tryptic in-gel digestion and by peptide mass fingerprint not only confirmed the identity of LYS1 in this band but also yielded peptides spanning the whole protein sequence, except for the first 53 amino acids (data not shown), thus indicating cleavage of the LYS1-GFP fusion protein between LYS1 and GFP.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of the protein band.

claim: The LC-MS/MS analysis indicates cleavage of the LYS1-GFP fusion protein between LYS1 and GFP.
source: Analysis of this major cleavage product by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) after tryptic in-gel digestion and by peptide mass fingerprint not only confirmed the identity of LYS1 in this band but also yielded peptides spanning the whole protein sequence, except for the first 53 amino acids (data not shown), thus indicating cleavage of the LYS1-GFP fusion protein between LYS1 and GFP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the peptide coverage from mass spectrometry.

claim: Three mutant lines with T-DNA insertions in the LYS1 gene did not abolish formation of the LYS1 transcript.
source: Three mutant lines with T-DNA insertions in the LYS1 gene were available from the Nottingham Arabidopsis Stock Centre. However, neither the insertion in the 5' untranslated region nor the insertions in the first intron and at the end of the last exon of the coding region abolished formation of the LYS1 transcript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two genetically independent LYS1KD lines have residual transcript levels not exceeding 10% of those detected in wild-type plants.
source: As proven by quantitative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), we obtained two genetically independent LYS1KD lines with residual transcript levels not exceeding 10% of those detected in wild-type plants (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The transcription of potential off-target genes was not affected in LYS1KD lines.
source: In contrast, the transcription of potential off-target genes was not affected (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of off-target genes shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant chitinase activity when compared with a Streptomyces griseus chitinase control.
source: Leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant chitinase activity when compared with a Streptomyces griseus chitinase control (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 4-MUCT assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild-type and LYS1KD plants exhibited only marginal chitinase activities.
source: In contrast, wild-type and LYS1KD plants exhibited only marginal chitinase activities.
evidence: This is demonstrated by 4-MUCT assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Enzyme activity was solely detectable in protein extracts obtained from LYS1OE plants in the zymogram assay.
source: Likewise, using 4-MUCT in a gel electrophoretic separation-based chitinase assay produced a zymogram in which enzyme activity was solely detectable in protein extracts obtained from LYS1OE plants, but not in those from control plants expressing secreted GFP (secGFP) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the zymogram shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LYS1 harbors the predicted chitinase activity.
source: Thus, LYS1 indeed harbors the predicted chitinase activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the chitinase assays performed.

claim: 4-MUCT is a typical substrate for lysozymes.
source: As 4-MUCT is also a typical substrate for lysozymes (Brunner et al., 1998), this was the first indication that LYS1 might also harbor lysozyme activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about lysozyme substrates, supported by a citation.

claim: Leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant PGN-degrading activity on M. luteus cells.
source: Next, leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants were tested for their ability to solubilize complex PGN presented by intact Gram-positive M. luteus cells and to cleave preparations of complex, insoluble Bacillus subtilis PGN. Again, protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant PGN-degrading activity whereas wild-type and LYS1KD plants showed basal activity levels only (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant PGN-degrading activity on B. subtilis PGN.
source: Next, leaf protein extracts from LYS1OE plants were tested for their ability to solubilize complex PGN presented by intact Gram-positive M. luteus cells and to cleave preparations of complex, insoluble Bacillus subtilis PGN. Again, protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant PGN-degrading activity whereas wild-type and LYS1KD plants showed basal activity levels only (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Wild-type and LYS1KD plants showed basal PGN-degrading activity levels only.
source: Again, protein extracts from LYS1OE plants exhibited significant PGN-degrading activity whereas wild-type and LYS1KD plants showed basal activity levels only (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assays shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: PGN-solubilizing activity profiles of protoplast suspensions confirmed significant PGN-degrading activity of LYS1OE plants.
source: Likewise, PGN-solubilizing activity profiles of protoplast suspensions derived from these transgenics confirmed significant PGN-degrading activity of LYS1OE plants (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by protoplast assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: LYS1 harbors hydrolytic activity for chitin as well as for PGN of the lysine-type (M. luteus) and diaminopimelic acid-type (B. subtilis).
source: In sum, we provide biochemical evidence that LYS1 harbors hydrolytic activity for chitin as well as for PGN of the lysine-type (M. luteus) and diaminopimelic acid-type (B. subtilis).
evidence: This is based on the enzymatic assays performed with different substrates.

claim: LYS1 failed to exhibit activity on cellobiose as a substrate.
source: Importantly, LYS1 failed to exhibit activity on cellobiose as a substrate, indicating it might have no cellulose activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cellulase assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: LYS1 resembles enzymatic activities reported for metazoan lysozymes and should be classified as lysozyme (EC 3.2.1.17) instead of chitinase (EC 3.2.1.14).
source: Thus, LYS1 resembles enzymatic activities reported for metazoan lysozymes and should be classified as lysozyme (EC 3.2.1.17) instead of chitinase (EC 3.2.1.14).
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate specificity and enzymatic properties of LYS1.

claim: The 4-MUCT assay yielded a Km of 70 ± 14 µM and a Vmax of 378 ± 42 µM min−1 mg−1 for LYS1.
source: The 4-MUCT assay yielded a Michaelis constant (Km) of 70 ± 14 µM and a Vmax of 378 ± 42 µM min−1 mg−1 for LYS1, and a Km of 53 ± 27 µM and a Vmax of 397 ± 145 µM min−1 mg−1 for commercial S. griseus chitinase.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of purified LYS1.

claim: The 4-MUCT assay yielded a Km of 53 ± 27 µM and a Vmax of 397 ± 145 µM min−1 mg−1 for commercial S. griseus chitinase.
source: The 4-MUCT assay yielded a Michaelis constant (Km) of 70 ± 14 µM and a Vmax of 378 ± 42 µM min−1 mg−1 for LYS1, and a Km of 53 ± 27 µM and a Vmax of 397 ± 145 µM min−1 mg−1 for commercial S. griseus chitinase.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of commercial chitinase.

claim: Using the turbidity assay with M. luteus cell wall preparations, a Km of 18.2 ± 2.5 mg/ml and Vmax of 4.4 ± 0.6 mg mg−1 min−1 were obtained for LYS1.
source: Using the turbidity assay with M. luteus cell wall preparations, a Km of 18.2 ± 2.5 mg/ml and Vmax of 4.4 ± 0.6 mg mg−1 min−1 were obtained for LYS1, and a Km of 8.4 ± 0.8 mg/ml and Vmax of 192 ± 120 mg mg−1 min−1 for commercial hen egg-white lysozyme.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of purified LYS1.

claim: Using the turbidity assay with M. luteus cell wall preparations, a Km of 8.4 ± 0.8 mg/ml and Vmax of 192 ± 120 mg mg−1 min−1 were obtained for commercial hen egg-white lysozyme.
source: Using the turbidity assay with M. luteus cell wall preparations, a Km of 18.2 ± 2.5 mg/ml and Vmax of 4.4 ± 0.6 mg mg−1 min−1 were obtained for LYS1, and a Km of 8.4 ± 0.8 mg/ml and Vmax of 192 ± 120 mg mg−1 min−1 for commercial hen egg-white lysozyme.
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of commercial lysozyme.

claim: The Km values for LYS1 are comparable to the commercial enzymes.
source: The Km values for LYS1 are thus comparable to the commercial enzymes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the measured Km values.

claim: The majority of LYS1 activity was found in the supernatant of the protoplasts, suggesting an apoplastic localization of LYS1.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, the majority of LYS1 activity was found in the supernatant of the protoplasts, suggesting an apoplastic localization of LYS1.
evidence: This is based on protoplast fractionation experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both the LYS1-GFP fusion protein as well as free LYS1 was detectable in concentrated apoplastic fluids.
source: Both the LYS1-GFP fusion protein as well as free LYS1 was detectable in concentrated apoplastic fluids whereas the cytoplasmic mitogen-activated protein kinase MPK3 was only present in the total leaf protein samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis of apoplastic washes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The cytoplasmic mitogen-activated protein kinase MPK3 was only present in the total leaf protein samples, not in apoplastic fluids.
source: Both the LYS1-GFP fusion protein as well as free LYS1 was detectable in concentrated apoplastic fluids whereas the cytoplasmic mitogen-activated protein kinase MPK3 was only present in the total leaf protein samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transient expression of the p35S::LYS1-GFP construct in N. benthamiana resulted in labeling of the cell periphery.
source: Moreover, transient expression in the heterologous plant system Nicotiana benthamiana of the p35S::LYS1-GFP construct resulted in labeling of the cell periphery, whereas expression of a construct lacking the LYS1 signal peptide-encoding sequence yielded labeling of intracellular structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of a construct lacking the LYS1 signal peptide-encoding sequence yielded labeling of intracellular structures.
source: Moreover, transient expression in the heterologous plant system Nicotiana benthamiana of the p35S::LYS1-GFP construct resulted in labeling of the cell periphery, whereas expression of a construct lacking the LYS1 signal peptide-encoding sequence yielded labeling of intracellular structures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LYS1 signals co-localized to a large extent with the plasma membrane.
source: Use of the fluorescent dye FM4-64, a plasma membrane and early endosome marker (Bolte et al., 2004), revealed that LYS1 signals co-localized to a large extent with the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LYS1 likely operates in close vicinity of the plant surface.
source: Thus, LYS1 likely operates in close vicinity of the plant surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization studies.

claim: LYS1 has been previously identified within the Arabidopsis cell wall proteome.
source: Indeed, previous identification within the Arabidopsis cell wall proteome (Kwon et al., 2005) suggests that LYS1 acts in the plant apoplast.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous proteomic analysis.

claim: The plant apoplast is an acidic compartment (pH 5–6).
source: Since the plant apoplast is an acidic compartment (pH 5–6) (Schulte et al., 2006), we investigated whether LYS1 is active at physiologically relevant pH conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about apoplastic pH, supported by a citation.

claim: LYS1 is active at pH values ranging from 3.2 to 7.2.
source: Although active at pH values ranging from 3.2 to 7.2, a pronounced maximum of LYS1 activity was detected around pH 6 which coincided with the apoplastic pH of plant cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pH-dependent activity assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A pronounced maximum of LYS1 activity was detected around pH 6 which coincided with the apoplastic pH of plant cells.
source: Although active at pH values ranging from 3.2 to 7.2, a pronounced maximum of LYS1 activity was detected around pH 6 which coincided with the apoplastic pH of plant cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by pH-dependent activity assays shown in Figure 4F.

claim: N. benthamiana protein extracts containing LYS1-myc displayed in-gel chitinolytic activity.
source: Similar to the Arabidopsis LYS1OE leaf extracts, extracts from p35S::LYS1-myc expressing N. benthamiana leaves also displayed in-gel chitinolytic activity (Figure 5B) compared with extracts from control leaves expressing the viral silencing suppressor p19 only.
evidence: This is demonstrated by zymogram analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: N. benthamiana protein extracts containing LYS1-myc were able to cleave preparations of complex insoluble B. subtilis PGN.
source: Likewise, N. benthamiana protein extracts containing LYS1-myc were able to cleave preparations of complex insoluble B. subtilis PGN (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by turbidity assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PGN digests produced by native LYS1 yielded several characteristic peaks in HPLC analysis.
source: Only a few peaks could be detected in the supernatant of PGN incubated with a buffer control or with heat-inactivated LYS1. In contrast, PGN digests produced by native LYS1 yielded several characteristic peaks that were also detectable in the supernatants of PGN preparations treated with mutanolysin, which has been shown to cleave O-glycosidic bonds between GlcNAc and MurNAc residues in complex PGN (Yokogawa et al., 1975).
evidence: This is demonstrated by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Only supernatants from PGN digests produced by native LYS1 or mutanolysin induced FRK1 expression.
source: Importantly, only supernatants from PGN digests produced by native LYS1 or mutanolysin induced FRK1 expression whereas buffer controls or digests produced by heat-inactivated LYS1 did not release immunogenic soluble fragments from complex PGNs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Buffer controls or digests produced by heat-inactivated LYS1 did not release immunogenic soluble fragments from complex PGNs.
source: Importantly, only supernatants from PGN digests produced by native LYS1 or mutanolysin induced FRK1 expression whereas buffer controls or digests produced by heat-inactivated LYS1 did not release immunogenic soluble fragments from complex PGNs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Activation of immune responses by LYS1-generated PGN fragments was dependent on Arabidopsis PGN receptor complex components LYM1, LYM3, and CERK1.
source: Notably, activation of immune responses by LYS1-generated PGN fragments was dependent on Arabidopsis PGN receptor complex components LYM1, LYM3, and CERK1 as the respective mutant genotypes failed to respond to immunogenic PGN fragments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis of receptor mutants shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LYS1-released PGN fragments triggered medium alkalinization in cultured rice cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, LYS1-released PGN fragments triggered medium alkalinization in cultured rice cells, suggesting that immune defense stimulation by soluble PGN fragments is not restricted to Arabidopsis only.
evidence: This is demonstrated by medium alkalinization assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Immune defense stimulation by soluble PGN fragments is not restricted to Arabidopsis only.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, LYS1-released PGN fragments triggered medium alkalinization in cultured rice cells, suggesting that immune defense stimulation by soluble PGN fragments is not restricted to Arabidopsis only.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rice cells also respond to LYS1-generated PGN fragments.

claim: Release of immunogenic PGN fragments into solution occurred rapidly within 10 min of incubation with native LYS1.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, release of immunogenic PGN fragments into solution occurred rapidly within 10 min of incubation with native LYS1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Incubation of complex PGNs with LYS1 yielded the highest immunogenic activity of the digest supernatant after 30 min.
source: Incubation of complex PGNs with LYS1 yielded the highest immunogenic activity of the digest supernatant after 30 min, suggesting that at that time point the maximum amount of immunogenic PGN fragments was generated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Prolonged incubation with LYS1 resulted in a loss of activity with overnight digestion completely abolishing stimulatory activity of the PGN digest.
source: However, prolonged incubation with LYS1 again resulted in a loss of activity with overnight digestion completely abolishing stimulatory activity of the PGN digest.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LYS1 is capable of releasing immunogenic fragments from complex PGNs, but extensive or complete digest into PGN monomers or small PGN fragments appears to abolish the immunogenic activity of PGN fragments.
source: We assume that LYS1 is capable of releasing immunogenic fragments from complex PGNs, but extensive or complete digest into PGN monomers or small PGN fragments appears to abolish the immunogenic activity of PGN fragments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course data showing loss of activity with prolonged digestion.

claim: Prolonged digestion of PGN with mutanolysin diminishes its defense-inducing activity.
source: This result is in accordance with our previous observations that prolonged digestion of PGN with mutanolysin diminishes its defense-inducing activity (Gust et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: LYS1 harbors chitinase activity.
source: As LYS1 harbors chitinase activity (Figures 4A,B and 5B) and as LYS1 transcripts accumulate upon fungal infection (Samac and Shah, 1991), we first analyzed the role of LYS1 in immunity towards fungal infection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chitinase assays shown in Figures 4A,B and 5B.

claim: LYS1 transcripts accumulate upon fungal infection.
source: As LYS1 harbors chitinase activity (Figures 4A,B and 5B) and as LYS1 transcripts accumulate upon fungal infection (Samac and Shah, 1991), we first analyzed the role of LYS1 in immunity towards fungal infection.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Fungal hyphal growth and necrotic leaf lesions at infection sites were detectable in all plant lines tested (wild-type, LYS1OE, LYS1KD) after B. cinerea infection.
source: Fungal hyphal growth and necrotic leaf lesions at infection sites were detectable in all plant lines tested and hyphal outgrowth or cell death lesion sizes revealed no differences between wild-type, LYS1OE or LYS1KD lines (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Hyphal outgrowth or cell death lesion sizes revealed no differences between wild-type, LYS1OE or LYS1KD lines after B. cinerea infection.
source: Fungal hyphal growth and necrotic leaf lesions at infection sites were detectable in all plant lines tested and hyphal outgrowth or cell death lesion sizes revealed no differences between wild-type, LYS1OE or LYS1KD lines (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 7.

claim: Infection with A. brassicicola resulted in indistinguishable necrotic lesions in LYS1OE and LYS1KD transgenics compared to those observed in wild-type control plants.
source: Likewise, infection with the necrotrophic fungus Alternaria brassicicola resulted in indistinguishable necrotic lesions in LYS1OE and LYS1KD transgenics compared to those observed in wild-type control plants (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: Trypan blue staining and microscopic analysis of the infection sites did not reveal major differences in fungal hyphal growth among all lines tested after A. brassicicola infection.
source: Trypan blue staining and microscopic analysis of the infection sites did not reveal major differences in fungal hyphal growth among all lines tested (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microscopic analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Disease indices at day 11 after A. brassicicola infection were slightly increased in LYS1KD lines, but such subtle differences were not statistically significant.
source: Although disease indices at day 11 after infection were slightly increased in LYS1KD lines (Figure 8D), such subtle differences were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by disease index measurements shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The authors failed to detect a role for LYS1 in immunity to fungal infection with B. cinerea and A. brassicicola under their experimental conditions.
source: In conclusion, we failed to detect a role for LYS1 in immunity to fungal infection with B. cinerea and A. brassicicola under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the fungal infection experiments.

claim: LYS1 might still have a role in fungal defense under infection regimes other than the ones used or might be important for defense against other fungal pathogens.
source: However, these results cannot be generalized and LYS1 might still have a role under infection regimes other than the ones used here or it might be important for defense against other fungal pathogens.
evidence: This is speculation about potential roles of LYS1 not tested in this study.

claim: Two independent LYS1KD lines exhibited hypersusceptibility to virulent Pto DC3000 infection.
source: Two independent LYS1KD lines exhibited hypersusceptibility to bacterial infection (Figure 9A), suggesting that lack of PGN-degrading activity results in reduced plant immunity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by bacterial growth assays shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Lack of PGN-degrading activity results in reduced plant immunity.
source: Two independent LYS1KD lines exhibited hypersusceptibility to bacterial infection (Figure 9A), suggesting that lack of PGN-degrading activity results in reduced plant immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hypersusceptibility of LYS1KD lines.

claim: Immunity to hypovirulent Pto DC3000 ΔAvrPto/PtoB was compromised in LYS1KD lines.
source: Likewise, immunity to hypovirulent Pto DC3000 ΔAvrPto/PtoB was compromised in these lines (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bacterial growth assays shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Expression of the immune marker gene FRK1 upon administration of complex PGNs was greatly impaired in the LYS1KD mutants.
source: Moreover, expression of the immune marker gene FRK1 upon administration of complex PGNs was greatly impaired in the LYS1KD mutants (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The enzymatic activity of LYS1 on PGN contributes substantially to plant immunity against bacterial infection.
source: These findings suggest that the enzymatic activity of LYS1 on PGN contributes substantially to plant immunity against bacterial infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of LYS1KD lines.

claim: Bacterial growth on LYS1OE lines was significantly enhanced compared with that observed on wild-type plants.
source: Unexpectedly, bacterial growth on LYS1OE lines was also significantly enhanced compared with that observed on wild-type plants (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bacterial growth assays shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: FRK1 transcript accumulation upon administration of complex PGN was strongly reduced in LYS1 overexpressors.
source: FRK1 transcript accumulation upon administration of complex PGN was also strongly reduced in LYS1 overexpressors (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: LYS1 overexpression does not affect transcript levels of LYM1, LYM3, and CERK1.
source: To exclude a direct effect of LYS1 overexpression on PGN receptor abundance, we examined transcript levels of LYM1, LYM3, and CERK1 but found no effect on the transcription of these receptor genes in the LYS1OE lines (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CERK1 protein levels were unaltered in the LYS1OE lines.
source: Also, CERK1 protein levels were unaltered in the LYS1OE lines, whereas there was no CERK1 protein detectable in the cerk1-2 mutant (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Susceptibility to Pseudomonas infection in the LYS1OE-3 line with moderately increased LYS1 levels was only slightly but not significantly increased.
source: Moreover, we included the LYS1OE-3 line with only moderately increased LYS1 transcript and protein levels in mature leaves (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B). Susceptibility to Pseudomonas infection in the LYS1OE-3 line was only slightly but not significantly increased (p=0.064, Student's t test).
evidence: This is demonstrated by bacterial growth assays shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lowering LYS1 expression levels, accompanied by lower LYS1 hydrolytic activity on PGN, brings LYS1OE lines close to wild-type susceptibility.
source: These results indicate that lowering LYS1 expression levels, accompanied by lower LYS1 hydrolytic activity on PGN, brings down these lines close to wild-type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the LYS1OE-3 line.

claim: Massive LYS1 overexpression and loss-of-function mutations are phenocopies of each other, irrespective of dramatic differences in LYS1 enzymatic activities.
source: Thus, massive LYS1 overexpression and loss-of-function mutations are phenocopies of each other, irrespective of the fact that LYS1KD and LYS1OE lines show dramatic differences in LYS1 enzymatic activities (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar susceptibility phenotypes of LYS1KD and LYS1OE lines.

claim: LYS1 contributes to plant immunity to bacterial infection by decomposition of bacterial PGNs and generation of soluble PGN-derived patterns that trigger immune activation in a LYM1-LYM3-CERK1 receptor-complex-dependent manner.
source: Altogether, we propose that LYS1 contributes to plant immunity to bacterial infection by decomposition of bacterial PGNs and generation of soluble PGN-derived patterns that trigger immune activation in a LYM1-LYM3-CERK1 receptor-complex-dependent manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Small ligand epitopes are crucial for binding to host PRRs.
source: Limited insight into the 3D structure of ligand–PRR complexes, as well as knowledge on ligand structural requirements for plant immune activation, suggests that small ligand epitopes are crucial for binding to host PRRs (Liu et al., 2012b; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural studies, supported by citations.

claim: Soluble fragments derived from complex microbial matrices serve as ligands for host PRRs and subsequent immune activation in both metazoans and plants.
source: It is thus generally assumed that soluble fragments derived from complex microbial matrices serve as ligands for host PRRs and subsequent immune activation in both lineages.
evidence: This is a general assumption based on structural and functional considerations.

claim: During bacterial multiplication and cell wall biogenesis, large portions of soluble PGN fragments are shed into the extracytoplasmic space from which only 50–90% are recycled.
source: First, during bacterial multiplication and cell wall biogenesis, large portions of soluble PGN fragments are shed into the extracytoplasmic space from which only 50–90% are recycled (Park and Uehara, 2008; Reith and Mayer, 2011; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on bacterial PGN recycling.

claim: Imperfect recycling of bacterial walls might serve as a source of soluble ligands for host PRRs sensing PGN.
source: This implies that imperfect recycling of bacterial walls might serve as a source of soluble ligands for host PRRs sensing PGN (Boudreau et al., 2012; Wyckoff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of incomplete PGN recycling, supported by citations.

claim: Muramylpeptides spontaneously shed by Shigella flexneri directly stimulate NOD1-dependent immune responses in mammalian immune cells.
source: Indeed, muramylpeptides spontaneously shed by Shigella flexneri directly stimulate NOD1-dependent immune responses in mammalian immune cells, and bacterial mutants impaired in PGN recycling hyperactivate host immunity (Nigro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Bacterial mutants impaired in PGN recycling hyperactivate host immunity.
source: Indeed, muramylpeptides spontaneously shed by Shigella flexneri directly stimulate NOD1-dependent immune responses in mammalian immune cells, and bacterial mutants impaired in PGN recycling hyperactivate host immunity (Nigro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Host lysozyme activity has been demonstrated to generate soluble PGN ligands for NOD2 receptor-mediated immune activation and clearance of Streptococcus pneumoniae colonization in mice.
source: Second, host lysozyme activity has been demonstrated to generate soluble PGN ligands for NOD2 receptor-mediated immune activation and clearance of Streptococcus pneumoniae colonization in mice (Callewaert and Michiels, 2010; Clarke and Weiser, 2011; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Davis et al. (2011) established a role for host lysozymes in PGN release from bacteria in the absence of detectable bacterial lysis.
source: Importantly, Davis et al. (2011) established a role for host lysozymes in PGN release from bacteria in the absence of detectable bacterial lysis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Drosophila Gram-negative bacteria-derived binding protein 1 (GNBP1) was shown to possess PGN-hydrolyzing activity and to deliver fragmented PGN to the PGN sensor, PGRP-SA.
source: Likewise, Drosophila Gram-negative bacteria-derived binding protein 1 (GNBP1) was shown to possess PGN-hydrolyzing activity and to deliver fragmented PGN to the PGN sensor, PGRP-SA (Filipe et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both passive and active mechanisms of PGN decomposition appear to occur simultaneously during host pathogen encounters and might not be mutually exclusive.
source: Thus, both passive and active mechanisms of PGN decomposition appear to occur simultaneously during host pathogen encounters and might not be mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence for both spontaneous shedding and enzymatic degradation of PGN.

claim: LYS1 constitutes the first plant lysozyme-type activity for which a role in host immunity has been established.
source: LYS1 constitutes the first plant lysozyme-type activity for which a role in host immunity has been established.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study.

claim: LYS1 is capable of generating immunogenic fragments from complex PGNs, which themselves serve as ligands for the LYM1-LYM3-CERK1-PGN recognition complex in Arabidopsis.
source: LYS1 is capable of generating immunogenic fragments from complex PGNs, which themselves serve as ligands for the LYM1-LYM3-CERK1-PGN recognition complex in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments showing that LYS1-generated fragments trigger immune responses in a receptor-dependent manner.

claim: LYM1 and LYM3 are PGN recognition proteins that lack apparent intrinsic PGN-degrading activity.
source: It is noteworthy that LYM1 and LYM3 are PGN recognition proteins that lack apparent intrinsic PGN-degrading activity.
evidence: This is based on the enzymatic assays showing no PGN-degrading activity for LYM1 and LYM3.

claim: Metazoans and plants employ hydrolytic activities for the decomposition of bacterial PGNs during host immune activation.
source: We conclude that metazoans and plants employ hydrolytic activities for the decomposition of bacterial PGNs during host immune activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study and comparison with metazoan systems.

claim: Host-mediated degradation of bacterial PGNs constitutes a conserved feature of innate immunity in metazoans and plants.
source: In addition to the established role of PGNs in pattern-triggered immune activation, host-mediated degradation of bacterial PGNs constitutes another conserved feature of innate immunity in both lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study and comparison with metazoan systems.

claim: The molecular components involved in PGN-mediated immunity differ structurally among phyla, suggesting both facets of PGN-mediated immunity might have evolved convergently.
source: However, as the molecular components involved differ structurally among phyla, both facets of PGN-mediated immunity might have evolved convergently.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary origin of PGN-mediated immunity based on structural differences.

claim: The most compelling explanation for the hypersusceptibility phenotype of LYS1OE plants is that PGN hyperdegradation results in fragments too small to trigger immune responses.
source: The most compelling explanation for this phenotype is that PGN hyperdegradation (in LYS1OE plants) or lack of PGN degradation (in LYSKD mutants) are equally disadvantageous to plant immunity and that immune activation in Arabidopsis requires oligomeric PGN fragments of a particular minimum degree of polymerization (DP).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of LYS1OE and LYS1KD lines and the kinetics of PGN fragment generation.

claim: Immune activation in Arabidopsis requires oligomeric PGN fragments of a particular minimum degree of polymerization (DP).
source: The most compelling explanation for this phenotype is that PGN hyperdegradation (in LYS1OE plants) or lack of PGN degradation (in LYSKD mutants) are equally disadvantageous to plant immunity and that immune activation in Arabidopsis requires oligomeric PGN fragments of a particular minimum degree of polymerization (DP).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes and the observation that prolonged digestion abolishes immunogenic activity.

claim: Immunogenic activities of fungal chitin or oomycete glucans have been reported to require defined minimum ligand sizes with a minimum DP of >5.
source: Likewise, immunogenic activities of fungal chitin or oomycete glucans have been reported to require defined minimum ligand sizes with a minimum DP of >5 (Cheong et al., 1991; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LYS1 overexpression might result in PGN fragments of insufficient size, thereby mimicking the physiological status in LYS1KD mutants lacking major PGN hydrolytic activities.
source: We therefore propose that LYS1 overexpression might result in PGN fragments of insufficient size, thereby mimicking the physiological status in LYS1KD mutants lacking major PGN hydrolytic activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar phenotypes of LYS1OE and LYS1KD lines.

claim: Plants produce various carbohydrate-degrading hydrolytic enzyme activities, some of which have been implicated in plant immunity to microbial infection, such as glucanases and chitinases.
source: Plants produce various carbohydrate-degrading hydrolytic enzyme activities, some of which have been implicated in plant immunity to microbial infection, such as glucanases and chitinases (van Loon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: It is widely assumed that plant hydrolytic enzymes contribute to immunity due to microcidal activities.
source: While it is often not entirely clear how these enzymes contribute to plant immunity, it is widely assumed that this is due to microcidal activities of these proteins.
evidence: This is a statement about the general assumption in the field.

claim: Arabidopsis LYS1 cleaves O-glycosidic bonds formed between GlcNAc (indicative of chitinolytic activity) as well as those formed between GlcNAc and MurNAc (indicative of peptidoglycanolytic activity).
source: In our study we have shown that Arabidopsis LYS1 cleaves O-glycosidic bonds formed between GlcNAc (indicative of chitinolytic activity) as well as those formed between GlcNAc and MurNAc (indicative of peptidoglycanolytic activity).
evidence: This is based on the enzymatic assays performed in the study.

claim: The authors have been unable to demonstrate any deleterious effect of LYS1 overexpression on fungal infections with B. cinerea and A. brassicicola.
source: However, we have been unable to demonstrate any deleterious effect of LYS1 overexpression on fungal infections, suggesting that B. cinerea and A. brassicicola at least are not affected by LYS1 function.
evidence: This is based on the fungal infection experiments.

claim: The authors have been unable to demonstrate direct bactericidal activity of LYS1 to P. syringae.
source: Likewise, we have been unable to demonstrate direct bactericidal activity of LYS1 to P. syringae (not shown), suggesting that the positive role of LYS1 in plant immunity to bacterial infection is not due to its direct inhibitory effect on bacterial fitness.
evidence: This is based on bactericidal assays (data not shown).

claim: The positive role of LYS1 in plant immunity to bacterial infection is not due to its direct inhibitory effect on bacterial fitness.
source: Likewise, we have been unable to demonstrate direct bactericidal activity of LYS1 to P. syringae (not shown), suggesting that the positive role of LYS1 in plant immunity to bacterial infection is not due to its direct inhibitory effect on bacterial fitness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of direct bactericidal activity.

claim: The findings are in agreement with a predominant role of LYS1 in the generation of PGN fragments that subsequently can trigger plant immunity via PRRs.
source: We would like to emphasize, however, that our findings are in agreement with a predominant role of LYS1 in the generation of PGN fragments that subsequently can trigger plant immunity via PRRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Plant LYS1 functionally resembles recently described mammalian lysozymes that were shown to generate soluble PGN fragments for PGN receptor NOD2, thereby mediating immunity to S. pneumoniae infection in mice.
source: Hence, plant LYS1 functionally resembles recently described mammalian lysozymes that were shown to generate soluble PGN fragments for PGN receptor NOD2, thereby mediating immunity to S. pneumoniae infection in mice (Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison with mammalian systems, supported by a citation.

claim: LYS1 gene expression is strongly enhanced upon PAMP administration or bacterial infection while expression levels in naive plants are low.
source: LYS1 gene expression is strongly enhanced upon PAMP administration or bacterial infection while expression levels in naive plants are low.
evidence: This is based on the expression analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The low constitutive LYS1 levels are sufficient to generate soluble PGN fragments from bulk PGN-containing bacterial walls which are then perceived via the LYM1-LYM3-CERK1 receptor complex.
source: It is conceivable that the low constitutive LYS1 levels are sufficient to generate soluble PGN fragments from bulk PGN-containing bacterial walls which are then perceived via the LYM1-LYM3-CERK1 receptor complex.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of basal LYS1 levels.

claim: The pathogen-inducible later increase in LYS1 activity could have further roles for generating diffusible signals that might serve innate immune activation in cells adjacent to infection sites.
source: It is possible that the pathogen-inducible later increase in LYS1 activity could have further roles for generating diffusible signals that might serve innate immune activation, not only in cells that are directly in contact with invading microbes but also in cell layers adjacent to infection sites.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential role of induced LYS1 expression.

claim: A role for plant glycosyl hydrolases in immunogenic PAMP generation and immune activation has been proposed previously.
source: A role for plant glycosyl hydrolases in immunogenic PAMP generation and immune activation has been proposed previously (Mithöfer et al., 2000; Fliegmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An extracellular soluble bipartite soybean glucan binding protein (GBP) was shown to harbor 1,3-β-glucanase activity and binding activity for glucan fragments of DP >6 derived from intact glucans.
source: An extracellular soluble bipartite soybean glucan binding protein (GBP) was shown to harbor 1,3-β-glucanase activity and binding activity for glucan fragments of DP >6 derived from intact glucans.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Complex glucans constitute major constituents of various Phytophthora species, many of which are plant pathogens.
source: Complex glucans constitute major constituents of various Phytophthora species, many of which are plant pathogens (Kroon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: During infection, GBP endoglucanase activity produces soluble Phytophthora-derived oligoglucoside fragments as ligands for the high-affinity binding site within this protein.
source: It was therefore suggested that, during infection, GBP endoglucanase activity produces soluble Phytophthora-derived oligoglucoside fragments as ligands for the high-affinity binding site within this protein (Fliegmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Causal evidence for the involvement of the endoglucanase activity in plant immunity was not provided in the GBP study.
source: While this study supported the concept of plant hydrolases tailor-making ligands for plant PRRs, causal evidence for the involvement of the endoglucanase activity in plant immunity was not provided.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous research.

claim: Eukaryotic PGN recognition proteins (PGRP, PGLYRP) are conserved from insects to mammals, bind PGN, and function in antibacterial immunity.
source: Eukaryotic PGN recognition proteins (PGRP, PGLYRP) are conserved from insects to mammals, bind PGN, and function in antibacterial immunity (Cho et al., 2005; Bischoff et al., 2006; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Kurata, 2010, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some PGRP family members are non-enzymatic PRRs (NOD1, NOD2) while others possess PGN-degrading activities.
source: Some PGRP family members are non-enzymatic PRRs (NOD1, NOD2) while others possess PGN-degrading activities (Gelius et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2003; Bischoff et al., 2006; Dziarski and Gupta, 2010; Kurata, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PGN hydrolytic enzyme activities such as lysozymes have been ascribed functions in direct bacterial killing and in generating soluble PGN fragments as ligands for PRRs.
source: PGN hydrolytic enzyme activities such as lysozymes have been ascribed functions in direct bacterial killing (Cho et al., 2005) and in generating soluble PGN fragments as ligands for PRRs (Wang et al., 2006; Davis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Metazoans and plants employ hydrolytic activities for the decomposition of bacterial PGNs during host immune activation, but the molecular components involved differ structurally among phyla, suggesting convergent evolution.
source: We conclude that metazoans and plants employ hydrolytic activities for the decomposition of bacterial PGNs during host immune activation. In addition to the established role of PGNs in pattern-triggered immune activation, host-mediated degradation of bacterial PGNs constitutes another conserved feature of innate immunity in both lineages. However, as the molecular components involved differ structurally among phyla, both facets of PGN-mediated immunity might have evolved convergently.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating the findings of this study with knowledge of metazoan systems.
